blocks.text: 本期内容
Anthropic 是如何把服务每一个 Claude token 的 API 从 Python 重写成 Rust 的？

inlines.text: Anthropic 是如何把服务每一个 Claude token 的 API 从 Python 重写成 Rust 的？

blocks.text: 今天的嘉宾是 Katelyn Lesse，她负责 Anthropic 的平台工程，此前曾在 Stripe 带领工程团队。她的团队负责 Claude API，以及 Claude Code、Claude Desktop 等产品背后的基础设施。

inlines.text: 今天的嘉宾是 Katelyn Lesse，她负责 Anthropic 的平台工程，此前曾在 Stripe 带领工程团队。她的团队负责 Claude API，以及 Claude Code、Claude Desktop 等产品背后的基础设施。

blocks.text: 我们从 Anthropic 从 Python 单体架构转向 Rust 说起。Katelyn 解释了为什么在全球 CPU 短缺的情况下增加 CPU 容量并不容易，Claude 如何帮助工程师快速上手 Rust，以及团队如何用影子流量对照生产流量验证这次重写。就在今天，Katelyn 和团队发布了一篇关于他们从 Python 迁移到 Rust 的深度文章。

inlines.text: 我们从 Anthropic 从 Python 单体架构转向 Rust 说起。Katelyn 解释了为什么在全球 CPU 短缺的情况下增加 CPU 容量并不容易，Claude 如何帮助工程师快速上手 Rust，以及团队如何用影子流量对照生产流量验证这次重写。
就在今天，Katelyn 和团队发布了
一篇关于他们从 Python 迁移到 Rust 的深度文章。

blocks.text: Katelyn 带我们了解如今 Anthropic 的软件工程工作是什么样子，以及代码审查和值班（oncall）如何与智能体工作流配合。我们还聊到了这家前沿实验室的“软件工厂”、一位产品经理如何把功能上线到生产环境，以及 Anthropic 为什么用基于智能体的练习取代传统的编程面试。

blocks.text: 1. Anthropic 用大约五个月时间把 API 从 Python 重写成了 Rust。这个名为“Messages API”的接口对外承载所有 Claude 的 token 服务，Claude Code 和 Claude Desktop 也走它。该服务负责鉴权、分词、计费和安全性检查，然后调用 GPU 栈生成 token。它原本是一个 Python 单体服务，团队起初对 Python 做了优化，但发现性能开销依然很大，最终决定用 Rust 重写。整个过程由几名工程师参与，前后花了几个月，而且团队里没有人是 Rust 专家！

blocks.text: 2. 等等，这个单体服务当初为什么用 Python 写？2023 年时，Anthropic 还是一家研究公司，决定要做 API 时，搭建它的团队规模很小，而且很多人同时在做研究。当时研究人员主要用 Python，这让 API 很容易与推理及其他基础设施代码集成。类似地，OpenAI 的 API 最初也是用 Python 写的，后来重写成了 Rust。Anthropic 和 OpenAI 在 Python 单体服务上遇到了同样的难题：单体服务占用的 CPU 资源逐渐成为越来越大的负担。

blocks.text: 3. 这次重写没有 Rust 专家参与，也没有严格的代码审查。一年前，同一个团队为新服务选了 Go，因为团队成员能读能写这门语言。但到了 2026 年，他们觉得 Claude 的 Rust 水平已经足够好，而 Claude 也在重写过程中帮助工程师进一步了解 Rust。团队没有做严格的代码审查，但拥有一个“不公平”的优势：现有的 Python API 本身就是一套完美的测试基准。他们让新的 Rust API 以影子模式运行在当前 API 旁边，不断迭代，直到所有响应完全一致。此外，Katelyn 估计工程师只仔细看过大约 20% 的生成代码：

inlines.text: 4. Anthropic 有一个全天候运行的代码审查智能体。
公司为所有拉取请求运行了一个 Claude 代码审查分类器，由它来决定：
对于“机械性”的低风险改动，比如升级 SDK 版本或改用更新的模型，Claude 可以判定无需人工审查。修复不稳定测试也是如此，这种情况下由另一个 Claude 完成审查，然后合并并部署。
对于确实需要人工审查的改动，Claude 会评估风险，并结合额外规则来决定需要多少次人工审查。
Claude 会把 PR 转给对应的团队。

blocks.text: 5. 在 API 值班中，Claude 智能体比人更早收到告警。过去几个月里，一个 Claude 智能体一直在跟随 API 团队的 API 值班轮班进行训练。随着团队逐渐相信 Claude 能判断告警是“真实”还是“噪音”，他们现在让这个智能体先对收到的告警进行分类。长期目标是让 Claude 无需叫醒人类就能处理实际故障——但目前还没到那一步。在我们近期的深度报道中，我们详细介绍了 AI SRE 初创公司如何应对同样的挑战：AI SRE：它是什么，如何改变值班——以及它真的有效吗？

blocks.text: 6. Anthropic 新工程师的入职培训就是“跟 Claude 聊”。过去，科技公司的新员工会有“入职伙伴”，还有工程师给他们讲解系统架构，通常靠画方框和示意图。Anthropic 不是这样：Claude 连接着代码库和内部系统，工程师直接让它解释系统如何运作。Claude 甚至能制作交互式教程和可视化内容。这与 OpenAI 工程师用 Codex 做入职培训的方式很像，我们在与 Tibo Sottiaux 的播客节目中介绍过。

blocks.text: 7. 有一件事没有变：规划和协调依然必要。Katelyn 的团队要与推理、研究、安全和应用团队打交道。启动一个项目时，大量时间和精力都花在让所有人达成共识上。Katelyn 说，规划时间与“AI 之前”相比没有太大变化。普通工程师花在协调上的时间实际上比花在实现上的还多！

blocks.text: 10. 精通一门编程语言开始变得不那么重要。在 AI 出现之前，Katelyn 花了很多时间学习编程语言。我问她，如今 AI 让编程语言没那么重要了，作为工程师会不会觉得难受。Katelyn 指出，有些工程师本来就不太在意语言；而对于热爱语言的工程师，她说语言和框架本身仍然有很多工作要做。

blocks.text: 12. 对于晋升来说，“完成项目所需的时间”如今已没有意义。Anthropic 仍然设有职级和晋升流程。但当一个原本要花一年的项目，现在借助 AI 几天或几周就能完成时，完成时间就没什么参考价值了！Katelyn 说，他们会转而评估项目带来的影响，比如节省了多少 CPU 用量、延迟降低了多少，或者避免了多少起事故。

blocks.text: “这段话是写给那些因为担心自己的知识和技能不再重要而陷入身份危机的工程师的：智能体基础设施相关的问题能否被解决、多智能体系统能否攻克世界上最难的难题，你和你的一身本领都可能成为关键变量。你完全可以、也应该深入这些领域，学习新东西，形成自己的判断。这个领域里还有太多问题等着新解法。现在正是让你的技能大显身手的好时机，令人无比兴奋。”

blocks.text: In this episode
How did Anthropic rewrite the API serving every Claude token from Python to Rust?

inlines.text: How did Anthropic rewrite the API serving every Claude token from Python to Rust?

blocks.text: Today’s guest is Katelyn Lesse, who leads platform engineering at Anthropic and previously led engineering teams at Stripe. Her team owns the Claude API and the infrastructure behind products like Claude Code and Claude Desktop.

inlines.text: Today’s guest is Katelyn Lesse, who leads platform engineering at Anthropic and previously led engineering teams at Stripe. Her team owns the Claude API and the infrastructure behind products like Claude Code and Claude Desktop.

blocks.text: We start with Anthropic’s move from a Python monolith to Rust. Katelyn explains why adding CPU capacity is tricky due to a global CPU shortage, how Claude helped engineers get up to speed in Rust, and how the team used shadowing to verify the rewrite against production traffic. Just today, Katelyn and the team published a deepdive on their Python → Rust migration.

blocks.text: Katelyn walks us through what the software engineering job looks like today at Anthropic, and how code review and oncall interact with agentic workflows. We also get into the frontier lab’s “software factory”, how a product manager shipped a feature to production, and why Anthropic is replacing traditional coding interviews with agent-based exercises.

inlines.text: Takeaways from the conversation with Katelyn

blocks.text: Here are 12 interesting learnings on how software engineering is changing inside of Anthropic:

inlines.text: Here are 12 interesting learnings on how software engineering is changing inside of Anthropic:

blocks.text: 1. Anthropic rewrote its API from Python to Rust in around five months. The API called ‘Messages API’ serves all Claude tokens externally, as well as for Claude Code and Claude Desktop. This service does authentication, tokenization, billing, and safety checks, then calls the GPU stack to generate tokens. The service was a Python monolith and the team initially optimized Python, but found the performance overhead was still large. Eventually, they decided to rebuild it in Rust. It took a few engineers and a few months in total; all without anyone being expert in Rust!

inlines.text: 1. Anthropic rewrote its API from Python to Rust in around five months.

The API called ‘Messages API’ serves all Claude tokens externally, as well as for Claude Code and Claude Desktop. This service does authentication, tokenization, billing, and safety checks, then calls the GPU stack to generate tokens. The service was a Python monolith and the team initially optimized Python, but found the performance overhead was still large. Eventually, they decided to rebuild it in Rust. It took a few engineers and a few months in total; all without anyone being expert in Rust!

blocks.text: 2. Hang on, why was the monolith written in Python in the first place? Back in 2023, Anthropic was still a research company when it decided to create an API, and the team that built it was small, with a large crossover to Research. It was the case that researchers worked mostly with Python, which made it very easy to integrate the API with inference and other infrastructure code. Similarly, OpenAI’s API was also written in Python – and later rewritten to Rust. Anthropic and OpenAI faced the same challenge with the Python monolith: the CPU footprint of the monolith started to become a growing problem.

. Anthropic and OpenAI faced the same challenge with the Python monolith: the CPU footprint of the monolith started to become a growing problem.

blocks.text: 3. The rewrite was done without Rust experts on the team or strict code reviews. A year earlier, the same team picked Go for their new services because it was a language that team members knew how to read and write. But by 2026, they felt that Claude was good enough at Rust, and Claude helped engineers learn more about Rust during the rewrite. The team did not do strict code reviews, but had the “unfair” advantage of the existing Python API being a perfect test harness. They set up the new Rust API to shadow the current API, and iterated until all responses were identical. Also, Katelyn estimates that engineers looked closely at only ~20% of the code generated:

A year earlier, the same team picked Go for their new services because it was a language that team members knew how to read and write. But by 2026, they felt that Claude was good enough at Rust, and Claude helped engineers learn more about Rust during the rewrite. The team did not do strict code reviews, but had the “unfair” advantage of the existing Python API being a perfect test harness. They set up the new Rust API to shadow the current API, and iterated until all responses were identical. Also, Katelyn estimates that engineers looked closely at only ~20% of the code generated:

blocks.text: “As long as you can really boil something down to make it verifiable in some way, then you don’t have to look at every single line of Rust code that’s getting written.”
4. Anthropic has its own code review agent running at all times. The company has a Claude code review classifier running for all pull requests. It decides:

inlines.text: 4. Anthropic has its own code review agent running at all times.
The company has a Claude code review classifier running for all pull requests. It decides:
Does it need a human review?

For “mechanical” and low risk changes like an SDK version bump or using a newer model, Claude can decide there’s no human review needed. This is also the case for fixing flaky tests, in which case, another Claude does the review, then merges and deploys it.
How many human reviews does it need?
For changes that do need human reviews, Claude scores the risk and takes into account additional rules to decide how many human reviews are needed.
Which team needs to do a review?
Claude routes the PR to the right teams.

blocks.text: 5. A Claude agent is paged before a human for API oncall. For months, a Claude agent has been shadowing the API oncall rotation of the API team for training. As the team have gained confidence that Claude can tell if an alert is “real” or “noise,” they now let this agent categorize an incoming alert first. The long-term goal is for Claude to handle actual incidents without waking up a human – but they’re not there yet. We cover more on how AI SRE startups are tackling the same challenge in our recent deepdive, AI SRE: what is it, how could it change on-call – and does it work?

blocks.text: 6. Onboarding for new Anthropic engineers is “talk to Claude.” New joiners at tech companies used to have “onboarding buddies” and engineers who explained the architecture of systems to them, often by drawing boxes and diagrams. Not so at Anthropic, where Claude is connected to the codebase and internal systems, and engineers just ask it to explain how things work. Claude can even create interactive tutorials and visualizations. It’s pretty similar to how OpenAI engineers use Codex for onboarding, as covered in our podcast episode with Tibo Sottiaux.

blocks.text: 7. One thing that hasn’t changed is the need for planning and alignment. Katelyn’s team interacts with Inference, Research, Safety, and App teams. When kicking off a project, a lot of time and effort is spent on getting everyone on the same page. Katelyn says that planning time has not changed much from “pre-AI”. The average engineer actually spends more time coordinating than on implementation!

Katelyn’s team interacts with Inference, Research, Safety, and App teams. When kicking off a project, a lot of time and effort is spent on getting everyone on the same page. Katelyn says that planning time has not changed much from “pre-AI”. The average engineer actually spends more time coordinating than on implementation!

blocks.text: 8. Another thing that has not changed is two-pizza teams. Teams at Anthropic are still two-pizza teams of around 5-8 people. Katelyn says it’s because this is the right size for understanding a complex system and staffing an oncall rotation. Teams still own systems, and get paged. And it is a team – not an individual – that’s responsible for each system!

blocks.text: 9. Engineers at Anthropic spend a lot more time building tooling than before. Even on product teams, engineers are spending a lot more time building tools that help them to accelerate their own work. For example, an engineer on Katelyn’s team set up a Slack channel that runs a multi-agent team towards a single goal, even though it was not a task assigned to the engineer.

blocks.text: 10. Knowing a programming language well is starting to not matter. Katelyn invested a lot of time, pre-AI, into learning languages. I asked if it hurts as an engineer to consider that programming languages matter less these days, with AI. Katelyn pointed out that some engineers always cared little about languages, and for engineers who love languages, she says there’s still work to be done on languages and frameworks themselves.

Katelyn invested a lot of time, pre-AI, into learning languages. I asked if it hurts as an engineer to consider that programming languages matter less these days, with AI. Katelyn pointed out that some engineers always cared little about languages, and for engineers who love languages, she says there’s still work to be done on languages and frameworks themselves.

blocks.text: 11. Katelyn’s team phased out the coding interview after strong candidates kept failing it. Candidates who crushed other interviews were starting to fail the coding one because they no longer write code by hand. In the absence of a set replacement, the team is actively experimenting with interviews conducted together with coding agents. The design (architecture) and project deepdive interviews remain unchanged.

blocks.text: 12. For promotions, the “time to complete a project” is now meaningless. Anthropic still has levels and a promotion process. But the time taken to completion is pretty meaningless when a year-long project can now be done in days or weeks with AI! Katelyn says that they fall back on evaluating the impact of projects; for example, how much CPU usage was saved, how much was latency reduced by, or how many incidents were avoided.

blocks.text: Katelyn’s message to engineers with an identity crisis: humans have plenty of engineering to solve, related to agents. She has written about this in detail. The takeaway:

inlines.text: Katelyn’s message to engineers with an identity crisis: humans have plenty of engineering to solve, related to agents.

blocks.text: “This is for the engineers feeling an identity crisis because they think their knowledge and skills won’t be important: you and your skills can be the difference in whether or not agentic infrastructure-related problems get tackled, and whether multiagent systems can solve the world’s hardest problems. You can and should go deep in these domains, learn new things, and form opinions. So much of this problem space is wide open for new solutions. It’s an incredibly exciting time to put your skills to work.”
